Before the first live class you need two things on your computer: Python 3, the program that reads and runs Python code, and IDLE, the small editor that comes with it. IDLE is where you will type, save, and run every program in this course. It is plain on purpose: no plugins, no settings to break, and it shows your errors clearly.

The good news is that installing Python also installs IDLE. You only download one thing. Plan for about 15 minutes, and do it before class so we can start coding on day one.

Before you start

  • You need a Windows PC, a Mac, or a Chromebook that lets you turn on Linux. Phones and tablets will not work for this class.
  • You need permission to install software. On a school-managed laptop that may be blocked, so check early and tell your instructor if it is.
  • Always download Python from python.org, the official site. Other "free Python" download sites sometimes bundle junk software.

Windows

  1. Go to python.org/downloads (opens in a new tab) and click the big yellow Download Python button. The site detects Windows for you.
  2. Open the file you downloaded (it will be in your Downloads folder).
  3. Follow the prompts:
    • Newer releases install through the Python install manager. If a black window opens and asks questions, type y and press Enter to say yes to installing the latest Python and to the PATH question.
    • If you see the classic installer screen instead, tick the box Add python.exe to PATH at the bottom before clicking Install Now.
  4. When it finishes, click the Start button and type IDLE. You should see an app called something like IDLE (Python 3.15). Pin it to your taskbar so it is easy to find.

Watch out

On the classic installer, forgetting the Add python.exe to PATH box is the most common Windows mistake. IDLE still works without it, but typing python in a terminal will fail. If you missed it, run the installer again and choose Modify to add it.

macOS

  1. Go to python.org/downloads (opens in a new tab) and click Download Python to get the macOS installer (a .pkg file).
  2. Open it and click Continue, Agree, and Install. Enter your Mac password when asked.
  3. When it finishes, a Finder window opens showing a folder named Python 3.x inside Applications. IDLE lives there.
  4. Drag IDLE to your Dock so you can open it with one click.

Tip

Your Mac may already have a python3 command from Apple's developer tools. Ignore it. For this class, always open IDLE from the Applications → Python 3.x folder so everyone is using the same, current version.

Chromebook

Chromebooks run Python through the built-in Linux environment.

  1. Open Settings, go to About ChromeOS → Developers, find Linux development environment, and click Set up. Accept the defaults. This takes a few minutes.
  2. A Terminal window opens when setup finishes. Type these two commands, pressing Enter after each one:
  1. Open your app launcher and look in the Linux apps folder for IDLE. If it is not there yet, you can start it from the Terminal:

Watch out

If you do not see Linux development environment in Settings, your school or family account has probably turned it off. Tell your instructor before the first class so we can sort out another computer.

Check that it worked

Open IDLE. The window that appears is called the Shell. Its first line shows your Python version, and below that is a prompt that looks like >>>. Click after the prompt, type this line exactly, and press Enter:

Python answers right away:

Now try some math. Type each line after the >>> prompt and press Enter:

The Shell shows each answer on its own line:

If you saw those results, you are ready. The exact version number in the first line does not matter much: anything starting with 3 is fine, and 3.12 or newer is ideal.

What usually goes wrong

  • You typed the >>> yourself. The prompt is already there. Type only the code after it.
  • You see NameError: name 'Print' is not defined. Python cares about capital letters. It is print, all lowercase. Newer versions even add a hint: Did you mean: 'print'?
  • You see SyntaxError. Check that both quote marks and both parentheses are there: print("...").
  • You opened Python but not IDLE. On Windows, an app named just Python 3.x opens a black window with no menus. That is not IDLE. Look for the one with IDLE in its name.
  • A Python 2 version shows up. Very old computers sometimes have Python 2. Close it and install Python 3 from python.org as described above.

Bring your working setup to the first class. If you get stuck anywhere on this page, write down the exact error message (or take a screenshot) and share it with your instructor. A precise error message is the fastest way for someone to help you.

Six weeks from now you will have written dozens of small programs. If they are scattered across your Desktop with names like untitled3.py, finding last week's code when you need it will be painful. Ten minutes of organizing now saves a lot of hunting later. This page also covers how each class runs and how to get unstuck when your computer misbehaves.

How the class works

Class meets live online once a week for 1.5 hours. Each week is a module with three lessons:

  1. Notes explain the week's ideas with short, runnable examples. Skim them before class and reread them after.
  2. Code-along builds one small program step by step. In class we build it together; your instructor types, you type the same thing in your own IDLE.
  3. Practice has exercises that get harder as you go. Try each one before you open its solution.

A typical class goes like this: a quick recap of last week, new ideas with live examples, the code-along, then time on practice exercises while instructors answer questions. Keep IDLE open the whole time. You learn far more by typing the code than by watching someone else type it.

Tip

When you are stuck in class, paste your code and the full error message into the chat. "It doesn't work" is hard to help with. "Line 3 says NameError: name 'nmae' is not defined" can usually be fixed in seconds.

Make a class folder

Create one folder for the whole course, with one folder inside it per week:

Put it somewhere simple, like Documents on Windows and Mac. On a Chromebook, save inside Linux files, because the Linux version of IDLE cannot see your regular Downloads or Google Drive folders unless you share them with Linux.

Move the two files from the last lesson into setup/. Then open IDLE and use File → Open to open them from their new home, so IDLE remembers the new location in File → Recent Files.

Name files so you can find them

Good file names are short, lowercase, and describe the program. Use underscores instead of spaces.

  • Good: week2_mad_libs.py, ex3_temperature.py, rocket_launch.py
  • Bad: untitled.py, My Program FINAL (2).py, test.py

  • Always end with .py. A file saved as hello.txt or hello.py.txt will not run with F5 and will not get IDLE's colors.
  • Do not name a file after a Python tool. Names like random.py, math.py, or turtle.py can hide the real tool of the same name and cause baffling errors in later weeks.

You are probably in the Shell, not the Editor. F5 only works in an Editor window that holds a saved file. Use File → New File or File → Open first.

If you copy code from a word processor, chat app, or slide deck, straight quotes " can turn into curly ones “ ”. Python only understands straight quotes:

Delete the curly quotes and retype them in IDLE. Then it works:

I pasted code from the Shell and got "invalid syntax"

Code copied from the Shell often brings the >>> prompt along with it. A file that starts with >>> print("Hi") gives SyntaxError: invalid syntax pointing at the >>>. Delete the prompts and keep only the code.

Mac: python says "command not found"

Restart IDLE first, then restart the computer. If the problem survives both, note your operating system, the exact error text, and what you clicked just before it happened, and send that to your instructor before class.

Every app you have ever used, from a game to a calculator, is a list of instructions a computer follows in order. A Python program is exactly that: a text file of instructions, one per line. This week you learn the most-used instruction in the language, print(), and the habit that separates tidy code from a mess: comments.

How a program runs

When you press F5, Python starts at line 1 and runs each line in order, top to bottom, one at a time. It does not skip ahead or guess what you meant.

Swap the first two lines and the output swaps too. Order is everything.

Anatomy of print()

  • print is the name of a function, a built-in command that does a job. This one displays things.
  • The parentheses ( ) hold what you want to display.
  • The quotes " " mark the start and end of a piece of text. Programmers call text a string.

You can use double quotes "like this" or single quotes 'like this'. Pick one style per string and close it with the same kind you opened it with.

Text versus numbers

Quotes change everything. Inside quotes, Python treats characters as plain text and prints them exactly. Without quotes, Python works out the value first.

Notice the commas in the last two lines. When you give print() several items separated by commas, it prints them all on one line with a space between each one. That is why "I have", 3 comes out as I have 3 without you typing a space.

Controlling the output

print() has a few extra settings that help you lay out text exactly how you want.

Here is what each trick does:

  • sep="-" changes the separator between items from a space to whatever you choose.
  • end="" stops print() from moving to a new line afterward, so the next print continues on the same line.
  • print() with nothing inside prints an empty line, handy for spacing.
  • \n inside a string means "new line here." It is one character even though you type two.
  • Mixing quotes lets you put one kind of quote inside the other. Use double quotes on the outside when your text has an apostrophe, like "It's".

Tip

Want a quick divider line? Multiply a string by a number: print("=" * 20) prints twenty equals signs in a row.

Comments: notes for humans

A comment starts with #. Python ignores everything from the # to the end of that line. Comments explain why code exists, label sections, and let you switch a line off without deleting it.

The pickle line never runs because it starts with #. Turning code into a comment like this is called commenting out, and it is a great way to test ideas.

Writing readable code

Code is read far more often than it is written, by your teammates, your instructor, and by you next week. A few habits make a big difference:

  • Start each file with a comment saying what the program does.
  • Use blank lines to separate sections, like paragraphs in an essay.
  • Comment the why, not the obvious. # print hello above print("hello") adds nothing. # Banner shown before the game starts helps.
  • Keep lines short so they fit on screen without scrolling sideways.
  • Put one space after # and two spaces before a comment that follows code on the same line. This matches the official Python style guide.

What usually goes wrong

Forgetting the quotes makes Python think your text is the name of something:

Forgetting the closing quote leaves the string open forever:

Other classic slips:

  • Print with a capital P. Python is case-sensitive, so Print and print are different names.
  • Missing a parenthesis. Every ( needs a ). IDLE highlights the matching one when you type the closing bracket, so watch for it.
  • Curly quotes copied from a document. Retype them in IDLE.

When you see an error, read the last line first. It names the kind of error and usually tells you what is missing.

Further reading

  • Built-in functions: print() (opens in a new tab) — the official reference for print(), including sep and end.
  • PEP 8: Style Guide for Python Code (opens in a new tab) — the official style guide; read the sections on comments and blank lines.

Last week every program printed the same thing every time. That is fine for a poster, but a game needs to remember your score, and a quiz needs to know your answer. To do that, a program has to store information and ask for it. This week covers both: variables to hold values, and input() to get them from the person at the keyboard.

Variables: names for values

A variable is a name that points to a value. You create one with a single equals sign:

Read = as "gets", not "equals." score = 10 means "score gets 10." The line score = score + 5 would be nonsense in math class, but in Python it means: take the current value of score, add 5, and store the result back in score. This is called assignment, and the right side is always worked out first.

Notice that print(player) has no quotes. Without quotes, Python looks up the variable and prints its value. With quotes, print("player") prints the word player.

Naming rules

  • Names can contain letters, digits, and underscores, but cannot start with a digit. level2 works; 2level is an error.
  • No spaces. Use underscores instead: high_score, not high score.
  • Names are case-sensitive: Score and score are two different variables.
  • Pick names that say what the value is. lives beats x, and price_per_ticket beats p.

The four basic data types

Every value in Python has a type, which decides what you can do with it. You can ask Python for any value's type with type():

Type Short for Examples Use it for
str string "Maya", "42", "" Text of any kind
int integer 3, -10, 0 Whole numbers: counts, scores
float floating-point 2.5, -0.75, 3.0 Numbers with a decimal point
bool Boolean True, False Yes/no facts

A few details trip people up:

  • "42" with quotes is a string, not a number. It is just the characters 4 and 2.
  • 3.0 is a float, even though it is a whole number, because of the decimal point.
  • True and False must start with a capital letter and have no quotes. You will use Booleans constantly next week when your programs start making decisions.
  • Floats are stored in binary, so tiny rounding surprises happen: 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004. That is normal in every programming language.

f-strings: a neater way to print variables

Putting an f right before the opening quote makes an f-string. Anything inside curly braces { } is worked out and dropped into the text:

f-strings let you control spacing and punctuation exactly, with no surprise spaces from commas.

input(): asking the user

input() shows a message, waits for the user to type something and press Enter, and gives back what they typed:

Here is a run where the user typed Ada:

Put a space at the end of your prompt, like "What is your name? ", so the user's answer does not crowd up against the question mark.

The big catch: input() always gives a string

Even if the user types a number, input() hands you a string. Watch what happens when you try to do math with it:

Python sees "13" + 1 and refuses, because adding text to a number makes no sense. The fix is to convert the string to a number first.

Converting between types

Python has a function named after each type that converts a value into that type:

  • int() turns a string like "42" into a whole number. Given a float, it chops off the decimal part rather than rounding, so int(9.99) is 9.
  • float() turns a string like "3.5" into a decimal number.
  • str() turns a number into text so you can join it to other text with +.
  • + means different things for different types: it adds numbers but joins strings. That is why "5" + "5" is "55".

The usual pattern is to wrap input() inside the conversion:

What usually goes wrong

  • Joining a number to a string with +. "Your score is " + 95 gives the same TypeError as above. Use an f-string, a comma in print(), or str(95).
  • Converting something that is not a number. If the user types twelve, int() gives up with ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'twelve'. Typing 3.5 into int() causes the same error. Use float() when decimals are allowed.
  • Using a variable before creating it. Python runs top to bottom, so print(total) before total = 10 gives a NameError.
  • Typos in names. scroe is not score. IDLE will not catch it until you run the program.

Further reading

  • Built-in types (opens in a new tab) — the official reference for int, float, str, and bool.
  • Fancier output formatting with f-strings (opens in a new tab) — the official tutorial's section on f-strings.
  • Automate the Boring Stuff, Chapter 1 (opens in a new tab) — covers variables, data types, input(), and str()/int()/float() with lots of examples.

A thermostat turns the heat on when it is cold. A game says "Game over" when your lives hit zero. A website hides the checkout button until your cart has something in it. Every one of those is a program asking a yes/no question and choosing what to do next. This week your programs learn to make choices too.

Arithmetic operators

You have already used +, -, *, and /. Python has three more that turn out to be surprisingly useful:

Operator Name 7 ? 2 gives
+ add 9
- subtract 5
* multiply 14
/ divide (always a float) 3.5
// floor divide (drop the remainder) 3
% modulo (just the remainder) 1
** power 49

// and % are a team. // answers "how many whole groups?" and % answers "how many are left over?" Here they convert minutes into hours:

% is also the standard way to test whether a number is even: n % 2 is 0 for even numbers and 1 for odd ones.

Order of operations

Python follows the same order you learned in math class: parentheses first, then **, then *, /, //, %, and finally + and -. Operators at the same level go left to right.

When in doubt, add parentheses. They make your intent obvious.

Comparison operators

A comparison asks a question and answers with a Boolean, True or False:

The six comparisons are == (equal), != (not equal), <, >, <=, and >=. Note the double equals sign for "is equal to." A single = stores a value; == asks a question. String comparisons are exact, so "cat" == "Cat" is False because of the capital C.

if, elif, and else

An if statement runs a block of code only when its condition is True:

Four runs with different temperatures:

How it works:

  • Python checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs the block under the first one that is True. Then it skips the rest of the chain.
  • elif (short for "else if") adds another condition to check. You can have as many as you need.
  • else has no condition. It catches everything that did not match. It is optional.
  • Each condition line ends with a colon :.
  • The code that belongs to a branch is indented by four spaces. IDLE indents for you after a colon. The last print() is not indented, so it runs no matter which branch was chosen.

Order matters

Because Python stops at the first True condition, putting a broad condition before a narrow one can hide it:

A 95 should earn "Amazing, an A!", but 95 >= 70 is checked first and is already True, so the elif never gets a chance. Put the strictest condition first: check >= 90 before >= 70.

Combining conditions: and, or, not

  • and is True only when both sides are True.
  • or is True when at least one side is True.
  • not flips a Boolean: not True is False.

Here they are in a real decision:

The third if prints nothing, because has_ticket is True, so not has_ticket is False. When you mix them, not is applied first, then and, then or. Use parentheses to make longer conditions clear.

What usually goes wrong

Comparing input without converting it. input() gives a string, and Python will not compare a string to a number:

Fix: age = int(input("How old are you? ")).

Using = instead of ==. Python even suggests the fix:

Forgetting the colon gives SyntaxError: expected ':'. Forgetting to indent gives IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'if' statement on line 2.

Writing or like English. This looks right but is always true:

The color is blue, yet it prints "Warm color." Python reads this as (color == "red") or ("orange"), and a non-empty string like "orange" counts as true. Repeat the comparison on both sides:

Say your teacher asks you to print "Thank you!" for all 30 people who came to a fundraiser. You could type print("Thank you!") 30 times. Then they ask for 300. A loop saves you from that. You write the instructions once and Python repeats them as many times as you need.

Python has two kinds of loop:

  • A for loop repeats a set number of times, or once for each item in a group.
  • A while loop repeats for as long as a condition stays True.

The for loop

Here's what each part does:

  • for lap in makes a loop variable called lap. Each time the loop repeats, lap holds the next value.
  • range(4) produces the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3. That's four numbers, starting at 0.
  • The colon : and the indented line underneath make up the loop body, the code that repeats.
  • print("Race over!") isn't indented, so it runs once, after the loop is done.

One trip through the body is called an iteration. This loop has four iterations.

Watch out

range(4) stops before 4, so you never get the number 4 itself. Forgetting this is called an "off-by-one" error, and every programmer makes it. If you want 1 to 10, write range(1, 11).

Three ways to call range()

You write Numbers you get Meaning
range(5) 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 start at 0, stop before 5
range(1, 6) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 start at 1, stop before 6
range(10, 0, -3) 10, 7, 4, 1 start at 10, step by -3, stop before 0

The third number is the step, the amount added each time. A negative step counts down.

Looping over a string

A for loop can also walk through anything made of smaller pieces. A string is made of characters, so the loop variable gets one letter at a time:

The accumulator pattern: adding things up

Loops are great at building up a running total. You make a variable before the loop, then update it on every iteration:

Sample run (the user typed 20, 35, and 0):

total = 0 has to come before the loop. If you put it inside, the total resets to 0 on every iteration and you only ever get the last number.

The while loop

A while loop checks its condition, runs the body if the condition is True, then checks again. It keeps going until the condition is False.

The line fuel = fuel - 1 is the stopping condition at work. Each iteration moves fuel closer to 0, so eventually fuel > 0 becomes False and the loop ends.

Using while to check input

while really pays off when you can't know ahead of time how many repeats you'll need, like asking someone again until they give a sensible answer:

Sample run (the user typed 200, then -3, then 13):

Stopping early with break

Sometimes it's easier to write while True:, a loop that would run forever, and leave it with break once something happens. break exits the nearest loop right away.

Sample run:

Infinite loops (and how to escape one)

If a while condition never becomes False, the loop runs forever. This version forgets to change fuel, so it prints "Fuel left: 3" over and over:

Tip

If your program gets stuck, click the IDLE Shell window and press Ctrl+C. You'll see KeyboardInterrupt and the program stops. Then look for the variable your loop forgot to update.

for or while?

  • Do you know how many times to repeat, or have a group of things to go through? Use for.
  • Do you need to repeat "until something happens" (a correct guess, a valid answer, the word "quit")? Use while.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the colon after for ... or while ... gives you a SyntaxError.
  • Wrong indentation. Only the indented lines repeat. If a line that should repeat isn't indented, it runs just once, after the loop.
  • Off-by-one ranges. Check your first and last numbers by running the loop and reading what it prints.
  • Resetting a total inside the loop. Set it up before the loop starts.

We'll build it in five steps. Save a new file in IDLE called guess.py and run it with F5 after every step. Don't skip ahead. If something breaks, you'll know it was the last thing you changed.

Step 1: One guess, with a fixed secret

Real games use a random number, but random numbers are a pain to test because you never know the answer. A trick programmers use all the time is to hard-code the secret while building, and switch to random at the end.

Run it and type 30:

It works, but you only get one chance. That's where the loop comes in.

Step 2: Keep asking until the guess is right

We want to repeat "ask, then compare" until the guess equals the secret. We don't know how many guesses that will take, so this is a job for while.

Notice guess = 0 before the loop. The while line checks guess != secret before anything else runs, so guess has to exist already. If you delete that line, you'll get a NameError. Python is telling you it doesn't know what guess is yet. Starting it at 0 works because 0 can never be the secret.

Tip

Everything that should repeat (asking and comparing) is indented under while. If you un-indent the if block by mistake, Python asks over and over but never says "too high" or "too low".

Step 3: Count the tries

A counter is the accumulator pattern from the notes. It starts at 0 before the loop and goes up by 1 each iteration.

Step 4: Add a limit

A game with no way to lose isn't much of a game. We'll stop after max_tries guesses. The loop should keep going only while both things are true: the guess is wrong and there are tries left. That's and, which you learned last week.

Test the losing path on purpose:

The loop can end for two reasons, and the if after it works out which one happened. If the guess still doesn't match, the player must have run out of tries.

Python comes with a module called random. import random loads it, and random.randint(1, 100) gives a whole number from 1 to 100. Unlike range(), both ends are included.

Here's the finished game, with a friendlier intro and a "tries left" message:

One sample run. Your secret number will be different every time.

Tip

Seven tries is always enough if you play smart. Guess the middle (50), then the middle of whichever half is left (25 or 75), and keep halving. Each guess cuts the possible numbers in half, and 7 halvings get you from 100 numbers down to 1.

  • Typing a word instead of a number. If the player types fifty, the program crashes with ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'fifty'. That's int() saying it can't turn that text into a number. You'll learn to read messages like this, and guard against them, in Week 6.

Suppose you're keeping track of the quiz scores for a class of 25. You could make score1, score2, ... all the way to score25, but then working out the average means typing 25 variable names, and a 26th student breaks your program. A list fixes this. It's one variable that holds many values, in order.

Making a list

Put the items in square brackets, separated by commas:

A list can hold strings, numbers, Booleans, or a mix. [] is an empty list with nothing in it yet.

Indexes start at 0

Each item has a position number called its index. Python counts from 0, the same way range() does:

Index 0 1 2 3
Item "chips" "apples" "popcorn" "pretzels"
Negative index -4 -3 -2 -1
  • snacks[0] is the first item.
  • snacks[-1] is the last item, whatever the length. -2 is second to last.
  • len(snacks) is the number of items, 4 here. The last index is always len(snacks) - 1.

What happens when you go too far

There are three snacks, so the indexes are 0, 1, and 2. Index 3 doesn't exist. When you see IndexError, check whether you forgot that counting starts at 0.

Tip

The file path in an error message will show where your file is saved. Older versions of Python don't print the ~~~^^^ line. It's only there to point at the part of the line that caused the problem.

Changing a list

Unlike a string, a list can be changed after you make it. Here are the moves you'll use most:

Code What it does
snacks[1] = "grapes" replace the item at index 1
snacks.append("cookies") add to the end
snacks.insert(0, "carrots") add at index 0 and shift the rest over
snacks.remove("chips") remove the first "chips" it finds
snacks.pop() remove the last item and give it back to you
"popcorn" in snacks True if the item is in the list

Watch out

snacks.remove("pizza") crashes with ValueError if "pizza" isn't in the list. Check first with if "pizza" in snacks:.

Looping over a list

A for loop hands you each item in order. You don't need indexes at all:

The average uses len(scores) instead of the number 5, so it still works if you add a sixth score. Python also has the built-in functions sum(), max(), and min() for lists of numbers. Writing the total loop yourself first, though, shows you what sum() is doing for you.

Looping with indexes

Sometimes you need the position as well as the item, for example to number a list. range(len(chores)) gives you every valid index:

We print i + 1 so people see 1, 2, 3, even though Python is using 0, 1, 2 behind the scenes.

Updating every item

This trips up almost everyone the first time. Read both loops and guess what each one prints before you look at the output:

In the first loop, price is a copy of each value. Doubling the copy leaves the list alone. To change the list itself, you have to assign to prices[i], and that means looping over the indexes.

Building a list as you go

Common mistakes

  • Off by one: the last item is my_list[len(my_list) - 1], not my_list[len(my_list)].

Every program you've written so far runs from top to bottom like one long recipe. Once programs get longer, you start copying the same five lines into three different places, and then fixing a bug means fixing it three times. A function lets you write those lines once, give them a name, and run them whenever you want. You've been using functions since Week 1: print(), input(), len(). This week you make your own.

Defining and calling a function

  • def means "define". It's followed by the name, parentheses, and a colon.
  • The indented lines are the function body.
  • Defining a function doesn't run it. Python remembers the body and runs it only when you call the function with cheer().
  • Define a function above the place where you call it. Python reads from top to bottom, so calling it first gives a NameError.

Parameters: giving a function information

A parameter is a variable in the parentheses that gets its value when the function is called. The value you pass in is called an argument.

Arguments match parameters by position: the first argument goes into name and the second into emoji_count. If you pass the wrong number of arguments, Python stops with a TypeError.

Return values: getting an answer back

print shows something on the screen. return hands a value back to the code that called the function, so you can store it, do math with it, or pass it on.

When Python reaches return, the function ends right there. Any lines after it in the body are skipped.

print vs. return

This is the most common confusion with functions, so run this one yourself:

add_print shows 5 on the screen but gives nothing back, so x is None, Python's value for "nothing". add_return gives 5 back, and y stores it. If you need to use the answer later, return it.

Functions can return any type, including Booleans, and that makes if statements read nicely:

Variables inside a function stay inside

answer is a local variable. It only exists while double is running. To use a function's result outside it, return it and store it: result = double(21).

Reading error messages

That red text isn't Python being mean. It's Python telling you exactly what went wrong and where. The report is called a traceback. Here's one that goes through two functions:

Read it from the bottom up:

  1. Last line: what happened. ZeroDivisionError: division by zero.
  2. The line just above it: where it happened. Line 2, inside average.
  3. Lines further up: how you got there. Line 8 called report, and report called average.

The cause: Luis's list is empty, so len(scores) is 0. Python ran Maya's line fine, which tells you the code works in general and something about Luis's input is unusual.

Error types you'll meet

Error Example message Usual cause
SyntaxError '(' was never closed or expected ':' a missing bracket, quote, or colon
IndentationError expected an indented block after 'for' statement on line 1 the body under if/for/def isn't indented, or a line is indented when it shouldn't be
NameError name 'scroe' is not defined. Did you mean: 'score'? a typo, or using a variable before it exists
TypeError can only concatenate str (not "int") to str mixing types, like "You are " + 13. Use str(13).
TypeError greet() missing 1 required positional argument: 'name' calling a function with too few arguments
ValueError invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'twelve' right type, wrong value, like int("twelve")
IndexError list index out of range asking for colors[2] when the list has only 2 items

Tip

In IDLE, SyntaxError and IndentationError show up in a pop-up box before your program even starts, and IDLE highlights the problem spot in red. The real mistake is often at the end of the line just before the highlight, such as a missing ) or :.

A debugging routine

  1. Read the last line of the error. Copy the error type somewhere so you remember it.
  2. Go to the line number it names. In IDLE, Alt+G (Cmd+J on a Mac) jumps to a line.
  3. Print your variables right before that line to see what they actually hold.
  4. Change one thing at a time, and run again after each change.
  5. Still stuck? Explain the code out loud, line by line, to a friend or a rubber duck. You'll often hear yourself say the bug.

Watch out

No error doesn't mean no bug. If the program runs but prints the wrong answer, that's a logic error. Python can't spot those. You find them by testing with inputs where you already know the right answer.

For six weeks you've followed along with programs someone else designed. The capstone flips that. You decide what to build, and you use everything from this course to make it work from start to finish. Students who pick something they actually care about (their favorite video game, a sport, a tool they'd use themselves) almost always end up with the best projects, because they keep wanting to make it better.

The brief

Build a text game, quiz, or tool of your choice in Python that runs in IDLE.

Your program must use

Requirement Looks like
Variables score = 0, name = input(...)
User input at least one input() the program reacts to
Conditions if / elif / else that make a real decision
A loop for or while, for example a game round or "play again?"
A list storing questions, items, scores, rooms, or answers
At least two functions you define with def, and at least one that takes a parameter or returns a value

What you hand in

  1. A .py file that runs from top to bottom without crashing on normal use.
  2. A test table showing at least 6 inputs you tried, including unusual ones (a blank answer, letters where a number goes, capital letters, a number that's too big), with what you expected and what actually happened.
  3. One bug you found and fixed, written up in a few sentences: what went wrong, the error message if there was one, and how you fixed it.
  4. A short demo of 2–4 minutes in class, where you run the program and walk through one piece of your code.

Pick one, mix two, or invent your own.

Text games

  • Rock, paper, scissors, best of 5. Uses random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]), a score for each player, and a round loop.
  • Choose-your-path adventure. Each room is a function, and the player's inventory is a list. Can they find the key before running out of moves?
  • Word guess (like Hangman). Keep a list of letters guessed, show _ _ a _, and count wrong guesses.
  • Dice duel. Two players roll with random.randint(1, 6), and the first to 20 wins.

Step 1: Build a test table

A test table lists inputs you tried, what you expected, and what actually happened. Aim for at least 6 rows, and make at least half of them unusual inputs, the kind a real user might type by accident.

Good unusual inputs to try in almost any program:

  • Blank: press Enter without typing.
  • Different capitals: MARS, Mars, mArS.
  • Extra spaces: y or milky way.
  • Wrong type: a word where a number goes (three), or a decimal where a whole number goes (2.5).
  • Out of range: 0, -1, 999, or menu option 7 when there are only 3.
  • The edges: everything right, everything wrong, an empty list.

  • Clear names. Rename x, thing2, and a to names like score, guess, and item_price.
  • Every function has a name that says what it does, and a one-line docstring or comment if it isn't obvious.
  • Remove debugging prints like print("i is", i).
  • Friendly messages. Tell the user what to type ((y/n), 1-3, or done) and what went wrong when they make a mistake.
  • Readable output. Add blank lines with print() between rounds or sections.
  • No copy-paste code. If the same 4 lines appear twice, they probably belong in a function.
  • A final fresh run. Close IDLE, reopen your file, and run it once more from the start.

Step 4: Present it

Your demo is 2–4 minutes. Here's a structure that works:

  1. The pitch (20 seconds). What is it and who is it for? "This is a space trivia quiz for my little brother, who's obsessed with planets."
  2. Live run (1–2 minutes). Play through once. Include one unusual input on purpose to show it's handled: "Watch what happens if I type YES instead of y."
  3. One piece of code (1 minute). Show a function you're proud of and explain what it takes in and what it returns.
  4. Your bug story (30 seconds). What broke, how you found it, and how you fixed it.
  5. What's next (10 seconds). One feature you'd add with more time.

Watch out

Plan your demo inputs ahead of time and practice them once. If something crashes live, don't panic. Read the last line of the traceback out loud and explain what it means. Reading an error calmly is exactly the skill this course is about, and teachers notice.

Final checklist

Go through this before you submit.

Requirements

  • The program uses variables to store information that changes.
  • It uses input(), and its behavior depends on what the user types.
  • It has if / elif / else making real decisions.
  • It has at least one loop (for or while).
  • It uses at least one list.
  • It defines at least two functions with def, and at least one takes a parameter or returns a value.

Deliverables

  • A .py file that runs from a fresh start without crashing on normal input.
  • A test table with at least 6 rows, including unusual inputs, with expected and actual results.
  • One bug write-up: what happened, the error message (if any), the cause, and the fix.
  • A demo of 2–4 minutes: the pitch, a live run, one function explained, and your bug story.

Quality

  • Header comment, clear variable and function names, and no leftover debugging prints.
  • Messages tell the user what to type and what went wrong.

You started this course by printing one line of text. Now you're handing in a complete program that takes input, makes decisions, repeats work, stores data, and is organized into functions. That's real programming. Be proud of it, and keep building.
